title: Squirrels, Ahoy!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore squirrels across three groups: ground squirrels (prairie dogs, chipmunks, groundhogs, marmots), tree squirrels (eastern gray squirrels, dreys, scent glands, food caching, teeth, omnivory), and flying squirrels (gliding with a patagium, endangered Carolina northern flying squirrel). They cover squirrel migrations and stampedes, why squirrels were nearly extinct in America in the 19th century and were reintroduced to urban parks, Eastern gray squirrels as invasives in Europe and Italy, tips on feeding squirrels safely, the reason squirrels freeze in front of cars, and the origin of black squirrels in New York and Toronto. The episode ends with a listener mail from a Baltimore kindergarten class about the Three Sisters (corn, beans, squash).

segments.title: Opening banter and squirrel overview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on squirrels, their Latin family name Sciuridae, the roughly 300 species, and the Greek origin of the word squirrel meaning shadow tail. They discuss the bushy tail, the jaw muscle anatomy, and how genetics has reshaped squirrel taxonomy. They preview three groups: ground, tree, and flying squirrels, and share anecdotes about squirrels in Atlanta.

segments.title: Ground squirrels
segments.summary: The hosts describe ground squirrels, including groundhogs, prairie dogs, chipmunks and marmots, which mostly live on the ground and are more communal than tree squirrels. They mention the record Texas black-tailed prairie dog town and how ground squirrels use scent and alarm calls to recognize relatives.

segments.title: Tree squirrels, dreys and food caching
segments.summary: Tree squirrels such as the eastern gray squirrel build leafy nests called dreys and sometimes huddle together for warmth in winter. The hosts discuss their ability to rotate their hind feet to climb down trees, chasing as part of mating, and scent glands on their feet that help them find buried nuts. They note squirrels plant forests by forgetting seeds.

segments.title: Squirrel behavior, diet and teeth
segments.summary: The hosts discuss squirrels' opportunistic omnivorous diet, their continuously growing incisors that must be ground down, and reports of red squirrels tapping sugar maples. They also mention squirrels learning from one another and the squirrel's historical presence in Australia.

segments.title: Flying squirrels and gliding
segments.summary: Flying squirrels are nocturnal and glide rather than fly, using a patagium skin flap and tail as a rudder to travel up to 150 feet. The hosts compare this to wingsuit flight and mention the endangered Carolina northern flying squirrel, along with wildlife land bridges that help squirrels cross freeways.

segments.title: Chestnut-era squirrel abundance and mast trees
segments.summary: The hosts discuss an old saying that a squirrel could travel from Maine to Georgia without touching the ground because of abundant chestnut trees, and link squirrel population density to mast-producing trees such as chestnut, beech and oak.

segments.title: Squirrel migrations and 19th-century decline
segments.summary: The hosts describe squirrel migrations, large stampedes of thousands of squirrels after bountiful food years, and how squirrels were hunted as vermin and for food. Squirrels became nearly absent in America by the mid-to-late 1800s, then were reintroduced to city parks, notably under Frederick Law Olmsted, with Ernest Thompson Seton promoting kindness toward them.

segments.title: Invasive squirrels, feeding tips and car-dash behavior
segments.summary: The hosts note Eastern gray squirrels are invasive in Italy and have displaced Eurasian red squirrels in Britain, with most remaining in Scotland. They give advice on feeding squirrels safely, avoiding raw peanuts because of aflatoxin, and why squirrels freeze in front of cars as an evolved predator-escape response.
topics: squirrels freezing in front of cars

segments.title: Black squirrels of New York and Toronto
segments.summary: The hosts discuss black squirrels seen in Brooklyn and New York, explaining that the color comes from a recessive gene for abnormal pigmentation, that they are closely related to eastern grays, and that populations are denser on islands such as Roosevelt Island. They cite an Untapped Cities article and mention Toronto's black squirrels.

segments.title: Listener mail: Three Sisters from a Baltimore kindergarten class
segments.summary: A kindergarten class from Baltimore City writes about learning the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) planting method and asks for a future episode. Josh and Chuck thank them and promise a future episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for listener contact and close the show.
